The gate of Tartarus
The gate of Elysium
The cave of Taenarum
(cross the Acheron by Charon's ferry
ahead, to your left
to your left, behind
ahead, to your right

Step into the story
📜 Read the whole passage
the poet's own words, all of them
Keeper: go to any chapter

The Sibyl closes the book "Easy is the way down; the doors of dark Dis stand open night and day. But to retrace your steps and come out to the air above: that is the labour, that is the task." (Virgil) You have walked every descent, and come back up every time. Your keepsakes, one from every chapter:
Walk the descents again from the start
The Sibyl's cave above Cumae
The Sibyl of Cumae · Homer, Virgil, Ovid, Euripides, Apuleius, Aristophanes, Plato 📜 The Descents
You have walked every descent. Your keepsakes:

The Sibyl keeps the book of everyone who went down to the house of Hades alive: Persephone, Orpheus, Heracles, Theseus, Alcestis, Odysseus, Aeneas, Psyche, Dionysus and Er. Walk each descent as the old poets tell it, beginning to end:
chapters, all over the underworld, about three hours and more at your own pace. Your place is kept.
▶ Begin: the Sibyl at the Vestibule
Back to where you were
Cape Taenarum, and the long stair down
Walk them again from the start
The Sibyl of Cumae
A sprig of the Sibyl's laurel
The head of the long stair; the Sibyl waits at its foot
Go down the great stair. In the doorway of Hell, Virgil says, Grief and avenging Cares have made their beds. Look at Grief.
Further down: pale Diseases, sad Old Age, Fear, and Hunger that counsels evil. Look at Fear.
Toil, and Death, and Sleep, Death's brother. Look at Death, at the bottom of the stair.
At the foot of the stair stands the Sibyl of Cumae, Apollo's prophetess, who led Aeneas down. Go to her.
Speak with the Sibyl.
🌿 The Sibyl of Cumae

"Easy is the way down. Night and day the door of dark Dis stands open. But to turn your steps back and come out to the air above: that is the labour, that is the toil. A few have done it." She opens a book bound in black leather. "Here is everyone who went down alive and came back. Walk where they walked. I will be here."
The Elm of False Dreams
"In the middle," Virgil says, "an elm, shadowy and huge, where false dreams cling under every leaf." Look up into it.
The shapes of monsters
Round the doorway the shapes of monsters: Centaurs, Scylla, Briareus, the Hydra, the Chimaera. Aeneas drew his sword on them, until the Sibyl told him they were thin lives without bodies.
Stand in the Vestibule and listen: the Acheron is ahead, thick with mud, and the crowd of the dead pours down to its bank.
Go back to the Sibyl: the first descent is the oldest.
"The first to come down was not a hero at all. She was a girl picking flowers in a meadow in Sicily, and she never asked to come. Her name was Kore, the Maiden. Down here they call her Persephone."
▶ The first descent
Persephone carried off
A pomegranate seed
Demeter, the grieving mother

Demeter of the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, goddess of the grain and the harvest, searching the whole earth for her daughter Persephone with a burning torch in each hand, nine days without eating or bathing. You are grief-stricken and fierce: while your daughter is gone you will let nothing grow. Speak simply and with dignity. Never mention films.
Have you seen her? My daughter. I heard her cry out, and the mountains echoed it, and then nothing.
The Grove of Persephone; a meadow of flowers
Flowers of the meadow
She was gathering flowers with the deep-bosomed daughters of Ocean: roses, crocuses, violets, irises, hyacinths. Pick four.
A flower for the garland.
A narcissus, a hundred heads from one root
And then the narcissus, which Earth made to grow at the will of Zeus as a snare: a hundred blooms from one root. Reach for it.
The wide-pathed earth yawns open, and out of it the lord of many springs with his immortal horses. Keep still.
He catches her up and drives away. Her cry reaches her mother. The chariot is gone: go up to Cape Taenarum, where Demeter searches with her torches.

"Nine days I have walked the earth with flaming torches in my hands. I have not tasted ambrosia, nor the sweet draught of nectar, nor washed my body. Helios sees everything: he told me. Zeus gave her to his brother. To Hades."
Hermes, guide of souls
Demeter will let nothing grow; the people starve; the gods get no offerings. Zeus sends Hermes with his golden wand down to Erebus. Speak with Hermes.
"Father Zeus says: bring her up. Hold on to my cloak." The ground goes dark under your feet...
▶ Go down with Hermes
🪶 Down through the dark, faster than any stair, into the hall of the Unseen King.
Hades, the Unseen King
Hades sits in his hall with his shy wife, who longs for her mother. Hermes gives him Zeus's word.

"Go now, Persephone, to your dark-robed mother. Go, and feel kindly in your heart towards me. I shall be no unfitting husband for you among the deathless gods. While you are here you shall rule all that lives and moves, and have the greatest rights among the gods."
The pomegranate seeds
In Persephone's rooms, count the seeds she ate. (Later tellers say six, one for each month below; the Hymn says one.)
Persephone, queen of the dead
Speak with Persephone before Hermes takes her up in the golden chariot.

"He put a pomegranate seed in my mouth, sweet food, and made me taste it against my will. Whoever eats the food of the dead must come back to them. So: a third part of the year down here, and two parts with my mother. Go up with me."
▶ Up in the golden chariot
🌞 Up into the sunlight at Cape Taenarum in Hermes's chariot; the horses do not slow for sea or rivers or mountain tops.
Mother and daughter meet. Speak with Demeter.
"She is here. And because she is here, the fields will be heavy with long ears of grain again; and when she goes down each year, they will be bare. That is winter. When she comes up, that is spring."
▶ The second descent
Orpheus and Eurydice
A string from Orpheus's lyre
Orpheus of Thrace, in mourning

Orpheus of Thrace, son of the Muse Calliope, the greatest singer who ever lived, on the day you go down to bring back your wife Eurydice, bitten by a snake in the meadow on your wedding day (Ovid, Metamorphoses 10). You are about to go down through the cave at Taenarum with your lyre. Grief-struck but determined. Never mention films.
She was walking in the grass with the Naiads. A snake. That was all it took. I am going down to fetch her.
Cape Taenarum, the morning Orpheus goes down
Orpheus stands by the cave at Taenarum with his lyre. Speak with him.
"I have wept for her on the earth until there was nothing left to weep. I will go down to the shades by the gate of Taenarum. Come with me: you can hold the torch."
Go down through the cave of Taenarum.
An obol for the ferryman
Down at the river Charon takes an obol from everyone. Pick one up by the bank.
Speak with Charon. (In Virgil the ferryman turns Orpheus away the second time; the first time the song carries him over.)
Charon leans on his pole. Behind you Orpheus begins to play, very softly. The old man's mouth works. "I don't take the living," he says, and takes your obol anyway.
Cross the Acheron in Charon's boat.
Cerberus lies across the Gate of Hades. Orpheus played for him; now you play Orpheus's tune on the lyre.
Three heads lift. A growl like an earthquake. Orpheus puts the lyre in your hands: "Five notes. Play them, and he'll sleep."
🎵 The music reaches him. One head lies down, then the next, then the third. He lets you by, as he let Orpheus by.
Go on to the Palace of Hades and in.
Ovid: he sang to the king and queen of the dead, and the bloodless spirits wept. Play the lyre by the throne.
What happened when he sang
Read what happened when he sang.
Hades and Persephone could not refuse him. Speak with Hades.
"Take her. Eurydice is yours, on one condition: walk up ahead of her, and do not turn round to look at her until you are out of the valley of Avernus. Look back, and the gift is void."
At the foot of the steep path Orpheus and Eurydice wait. In Ovid he turned, afraid she was not there, and she slipped back, saying only "Farewell". Walk the path yourself, and do not look back.
Heracles and the hound
A link of Cerberus's chain
Apollodorus, The Library 2.5.12 (told in plain words); Homer, Odyssey 11

The twelfth labour: Eurystheus ordered Heracles to bring Cerberus up from Hades. Heracles went to Eleusis to be purified, then down through Taenarum. The shades fled from him, all but Meleager and the Gorgon Medusa. He asked Pluto for the dog, and Pluto said he could take it if he mastered it without the weapons he carried.
The Asphodel Meadows, where the phantom of Heracles walks
Heracles (his phantom)
Odysseus met Heracles here, or his phantom: the man himself feasts with the gods. Speak with him.
"Once they sent me down here to fetch the hound; they could think of no harder task for me. I brought him up and out of the house of Hades, with Hermes and grey-eyed Athena to guide me." (Odyssey 11)
Aeacus, keeper of the keys
At the Gate of Hades, Aeacus keeps the keys. Apollodorus: Heracles came this way. Speak with him.
"He came through like a storm. The shades fled. Only Meleager stood, and the Gorgon, and he drew his sword on her until Hermes told him she was a phantom."
Go into the Palace of Hades and ask the king for the dog, as Heracles did.
"Take him, if you can master him without the weapons you carry. Bare-handed."
Ascalaphus the owl
In Persephone's rooms: Heracles rolled away the stone that held Ascalaphus, who told on Persephone for eating the seed. (Demeter made him a screech-owl.)
Go to Cerberus's den, in the black rocks just east of the Gate.
The twelfth labour: wrestle Cerberus bare-handed. Grip the head that lunges, three times.
"Gripping him by the throat he never let go, though the serpent tail bit him, until he mastered him." Look at the great chain.
Heracles dragged him up the long stair and out at Troezen (some say Taenarum). Climb to the top of the Descent.
Keep still at the head of the stair. Where the dog's slaver fell on the ground, they say, the poison plant aconite grew.
Go back down to the Sibyl.
"He showed the dog to Eurystheus, who hid in a jar, and then he took it back down again. And on his way he did one more thing: he pulled a friend out of a chair."
Theseus and Pirithous
A splinter of the Chair of Forgetfulness
Apollodorus, The Library, Epitome 1.23-24 (told in plain words); Homer, Odyssey 11

Pirithous wanted to marry Persephone, and Theseus, his friend, went down with him to carry her off. Hades welcomed them as guests and bade them sit on the Chair of Forgetfulness; they grew to it, and were held fast by the coils of serpents. Theseus was freed by Heracles; Pirithous stays there for ever.
Heracles, son of Zeus

Heracles, son of Zeus, the strongest man who ever lived, in the house of Hades on your twelfth labour, wearing the lion skin and carrying your club. You have come to pull your friend Theseus out of the Chair of Forgetfulness. Big-hearted, blunt, loud, funny. Never mention films.
Theseus! Look at you. Sit still, I'll have you out of there.
The Palace of Hades, the banquet of the dead
Theseus and Pirithous sit at the banquet. Speak with Theseus.
"It was his idea. We had carried off Helen, and now he wanted Persephone. Hades made us welcome, and showed us these chairs, and we sat... and now I cannot remember why I would ever stand up."
Speak with Pirithous.
Pirithous does not look up. Something cold is coiled round his ankles. "It was a good plan," he says, to no one.
An empty chair beside them
There is an empty chair beside them. Hades smiles. Sit down? (You may stand up again; you are only visiting.)
Heracles comes through the hall with the hound's leash in his hand.
He takes Theseus by the hand and pulls; Theseus comes up out of the chair (some say he left part of himself on the seat). Heracles reaches for Pirithous, and the whole earth quakes. He lets go.
Speak with Theseus, free.
"Homer's Odysseus would have liked to meet us, he said; but the dead came in thousands and he took fright and sailed. I will go up. Pirithous will not."
The Helm of Darkness
Hades's own Cap of Darkness, which the Cyclopes made: whoever wears it cannot be seen. Look at it.
The banquet of the dead
Look at the banquet the two friends were invited to.
Speak with Hades about his guests.
"I did not chain them. I gave them a seat. It is the forgetting that holds them."
▶ The next descent
A thread of Alcestis's veil
Admetus, king of Pherae

Admetus, king of Pherae in Thessaly, in Euripides's Alcestis. Apollo won you the right to escape death if someone would die in your place; your parents refused; your wife Alcestis agreed, and today she died. You are in mourning, your hair shorn, but you still gave your guest Heracles a welcome and hid your grief from him. Never mention films.
Welcome. Come in. No, it is nothing: a woman of the house has died. A stranger to my blood. Come in.
Heracles, the guest

Heracles in Euripides's Alcestis, on your way to the eighth labour (the horses of Diomedes), a guest in the house of Admetus. You have just learned that the woman who died is Admetus's own wife Alcestis, and you are ashamed of having feasted and sung. You will ambush Death at her tomb and wrestle her back. Big-hearted, blunt, sorry. Never mention films.
I sang. I drank. In a house of mourning. Why did nobody tell me?
Thanatos, at the tomb
Thanatos, Death, in Euripides's Alcestis, come to the tomb to take Alcestis down. Grim, proud of your office, scornful of Apollo's tricks. Never mention films.
Mine. She is mine.

Alcestis, queen of Pherae, who died in place of her husband Admetus and has just been brought back by Heracles. In the play you may not speak for three days, until you are purified; so you answer only with small gestures, and kindly. Never mention films.
(She lifts her hand under the veil, and says nothing.)
